title: TCP U1·W3 — Gifting & Wealth-Transfer Planning (2026)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — moving wealth at the lowest tax cost

Beyond the income tax sits the transfer-tax system — gift, estate, and generation-skipping transfer (GST) taxes — and the planning to move wealth across generations at the least cost. For a successful owner like Jordan Reed, whose construction business and real estate appreciate over time, when and how to transfer assets can save enormous tax. This week covers the gift and estate framework on the 2026 Public Law 119-21 baseline, the GST tax, and the pivotal basis trade-off between gifting and inheriting.

The gift tax and the annual exclusion

The gift tax applies to gratuitous lifetime transfers, but several features make most gifting tax-free. The annual exclusion — approximately $19,000 per donee in 2026 (inflation-indexed) — lets a donor give that amount to any number of recipients each year with no gift tax and no use of the lifetime exemption; it applies only to gifts of a present interest (the donee's immediate use). Gift splitting lets a married couple treat gifts as made half by each, doubling the exclusion to about $38,000 per donee. The unlimited marital deduction (gifts to a U.S.-citizen spouse) and unlimited charitable deduction, plus direct payments of tuition and medical expenses, are entirely excluded.

The unified exemption

Gifts above the annual exclusion use the lifetime unified exemption, which the 2026 baseline sets at approximately $15 million per person (§70106, made permanent and inflation-indexed). The same exemption covers both lifetime gifts and the estate at death — it is "unified." A donor reports taxable gifts on a gift-tax return and reduces the remaining exemption; tax is owed only after the cumulative exemption is exhausted. Because the exemption is so large and now permanent, most families plan to use it efficiently — gifting appreciating assets early so future growth escapes the transfer tax — rather than to avoid an imminent tax.

The estate tax

The estate tax applies to the gross estate — everything the decedent owned or controlled at death (property, life-insurance proceeds on policies the decedent owned, certain prior transfers) — at fair value. From the gross estate, deductions (debts, funeral and administration expenses, the unlimited marital and charitable deductions) yield the taxable estate, against which the remaining unified exemption applies. A key planning feature is portability: a surviving spouse can elect to use the deceased spouse's unused exemption (DSUE), effectively giving a married couple two exemptions (~$30 million combined) without complex trusts.

The generation-skipping transfer tax

The GST tax is a second tax that prevents families from avoiding a layer of estate tax by transferring directly to grandchildren (or other "skip persons" two or more generations below). It applies on top of the gift or estate tax to such transfers, at the top transfer-tax rate, but each person has a GST exemption equal to the unified exemption (~$15 million) that can be allocated to skip transfers. Planning with dynasty trusts leverages the GST exemption so that wealth can grow and pass through multiple generations free of repeated transfer tax.

The basis trade-off — gift versus inherit

The single most important income-tax consideration in transfer planning is basis. A gift carries a carryover basis — the donee takes the donor's basis, so the built-in gain is preserved and will be taxed when the donee sells. An inheritance instead receives a stepped-up basis to fair value at death, permanently erasing the decedent's unrealized appreciation. This creates a genuine trade-off: gifting removes future appreciation from the estate (saving transfer tax) but forfeits the step-up (costing income tax). The rule of thumb: gift high-basis or rapidly appreciating assets, but hold low-basis appreciated assets until death to capture the step-up — the heart of integrated wealth-transfer planning.

Gifting strategies

Several techniques operationalize the framework. Annual-exclusion gifting to many donees moves wealth steadily with no exemption cost. 529-plan superfunding lets a donor front-load five years of annual exclusions into an education account at once. Gifting appreciating assets early (business interests, real estate) freezes their value in the estate while future growth passes tax-free. Grantor trusts, family limited partnerships, and minority-interest valuation discounts can transfer assets at reduced gift-tax value. Each technique balances transfer-tax savings, the basis trade-off, and the donor's need to retain control and income.

Coordinating with the income tax

Wealth-transfer planning never stands alone — it must coordinate with the income tax. Gifting an income-producing asset shifts its income to the donee (useful if the donee is in a lower bracket, subject to the kiddie tax on a child's unearned income). Charitable transfers earn an income-tax deduction and remove the asset from the estate. The integrated planner weighs the transfer-tax exemption, the income-tax basis step-up, the donee's bracket, and the donor's control — choosing the combination that minimizes the family's total tax across both systems and across generations.

Trusts as transfer vehicles

Trusts are the workhorses of wealth transfer because they separate control from ownership. An irrevocable trust removes assets (and their future appreciation) from the grantor's estate while letting the grantor set terms for beneficiaries. A grantor trust is taxed to the grantor for income tax even though it is outside the estate — so the grantor's payment of the trust's income tax is itself a further tax-free benefit to the beneficiaries. Irrevocable life-insurance trusts (ILITs) keep insurance proceeds out of the estate; GRATs and charitable remainder trusts split interests to transfer value at a discount. Because a trust's income is compressed into the top bracket quickly, planners often distribute income to lower-bracket beneficiaries (carrying it out via distributable net income). The trust choice balances estate exclusion, income-tax treatment, and the grantor's desire to retain control.

CMA bridge

For Jordan Reed, transferring MBG ownership to the next generation is a transfer-tax and basis problem at once: gifting business interests early freezes their estate value and uses valuation discounts, but forfeits the step-up the heirs would get by inheriting. The CFO who models the business succession this way — transfer tax versus basis, control versus exemption — delivers planning worth far more than any single year's deduction.

Practice and recap

  1. Use the annual exclusion (~$19,000/donee 2026, present-interest gifts; gift splitting doubles it) plus unlimited marital/charitable deductions and direct tuition/medical payments.
  2. Apply the ~$15 million unified exemption (covers lifetime gifts + estate) and estate-tax portability of the deceased spouse's unused exemption (DSUE).
  3. Apply the GST tax to skip persons, with a ~$15 million GST exemption and dynasty-trust leverage.
  4. Weigh the basis trade-off: gift carries over basis (removes appreciation from the estate); inheritance steps up to FMV — gift high-basis/appreciating, hold low-basis appreciated for the step-up.

Recap: wealth-transfer planning uses the annual exclusion (~$19,000 per donee in 2026 for present-interest gifts, doubled by gift splitting), unlimited marital and charitable deductions, and direct tuition/medical payments to move wealth tax-free, then the ~$15 million unified exemption (with estate-tax portability of the DSUE) for larger transfers, while the GST tax and its ~$15 million exemption govern transfers to skip persons; and the pivotal income-tax consideration is basis — gifts carry over basis (removing future appreciation from the estate) while inheritances step up to fair value, so the planner gifts high-basis or appreciating assets and holds low-basis appreciated assets for the step-up.

questions.q: The gift-tax annual exclusion applies only to gifts of a:
questions.explain: Only present-interest gifts (immediate use) qualify for the annual exclusion.

questions.q: Which transfer is entirely excluded from gift tax regardless of amount?
choices: Direct payment of a grandchild's tuition to the school
A $1,000,000 cash gift to a friend
A gift of stock to an adult child
questions.explain: Direct payments of tuition (and medical expenses) are unlimited exclusions, as are gifts to a spouse or charity.

questions.q: Under the 2026 baseline, the unified estate-and-gift exemption is approximately:
questions.explain: PL 119-21 §70106 sets the unified exemption at roughly $15 million per person, permanent and indexed.

questions.q: Property received by INHERITANCE takes a basis equal to:
choices: Fair value at the date of death (stepped up)
questions.explain: Inherited property is stepped up to FMV at death; gifted property instead carries over the donor's basis.

questions.q: For income-tax basis planning, a taxpayer should generally:
choices: Gift high-basis/appreciating assets and hold low-basis appreciated assets until death
questions.explain: Gifting forfeits the step-up, so hold low-basis appreciated assets for inheritance and gift high-basis or appreciating ones.

questions.q: The generation-skipping transfer (GST) tax targets transfers to:
questions.explain: The GST tax applies to transfers to skip persons (two+ generations below), preventing avoidance of a layer of estate tax.

questions.q: Estate-tax portability allows a surviving spouse to:
choices: Use the deceased spouse's unused exemption (DSUE)
questions.explain: Portability lets the survivor elect to use the deceased spouse's unused exemption amount.
